clinicalPearls: Characterised by a uniformly shallow or flat anterior chamber, both centrally and peripherally, with raised or normal intraocular pressure.
Classically arises after incisional glaucoma or cataract surgery in an eye predisposed by short axial length, a small anterior segment or nanophthalmos.
A patent peripheral iridotomy that fails to deepen the chamber effectively excludes pupillary block and points to aqueous misdirection.
Central to the mechanism is posterior diversion of aqueous into or behind the vitreous, pushing the whole lens-iris or vitreous face forward.
Medical therapy combines cycloplegia to tighten the zonules and posteriorly rotate the ciliary body, aqueous suppressants and hyperosmotic agents to shrink the vitreous.
Miotics paradoxically worsen the condition and must be avoided.
Nd:YAG laser disruption of the anterior hyaloid, often through an iridotomy or after capsulotomy, can re-establish a normal aqueous pathway in pseudophakic eyes.
Refractory cases require pars plana vitrectomy with disruption of the anterior hyaloid, sometimes combined with lens removal, to create a unified fluid compartment.
reference.pathophysiology: Aqueous humour is abnormally diverted posteriorly, becoming trapped within or behind the vitreous body instead of flowing forward through the pupil to the trabecular meshwork. A postulated ciliolenticular or ciliovitreal block, in which the ciliary processes rotate forward and appose the lens equator, capsule or anterior hyaloid, prevents anterior aqueous movement. Accumulating aqueous in the vitreous cavity raises posterior segment pressure, driving the lens-iris diaphragm or vitreous face anteriorly and flattening the entire anterior chamber. Because the block is at the level of the ciliary body and hyaloid rather than the pupil, peripheral iridotomy does not relieve it. Reduced vitreous fluid conductivity and a crowded, small anterior segment predispose to the self-sustaining cycle.
additionalDifferentials: overfiltration with a flat chamber and hypotony after trabeculectomy
wound leak with shallow anterior chamber
posterior segment mass pushing the lens-iris diaphragm forward
additionalInvestigations: gonioscopy and assessment of anterior chamber depth centrally and peripherally
ultrasound biomicroscopy showing anterior ciliary body rotation and iridolenticular apposition
B-scan ultrasonography to exclude suprachoroidal haemorrhage or choroidal effusion
anterior segment optical coherence tomography of the angle and chamber
axial length biometry documenting a short or nanophthalmic eye
redFlags: flat anterior chamber with raised pressure unresponsive to iridotomy
rapidly rising pressure after intraocular surgery in a small eye
features suggesting suprachoroidal haemorrhage requiring urgent differentiation
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and a stepwise medical, laser and surgical approach the anterior chamber can usually be re-formed and pressure controlled, but the condition is often recurrent and the fellow eye is at risk after any future intraocular surgery.
pitfalls: Administering miotics, which aggravate the anterior displacement of the lens-iris diaphragm.
Repeatedly performing or enlarging an iridotomy when pupillary block has already been excluded.
Missing an occult suprachoroidal haemorrhage that mimics the flat chamber picture.
Failing to warn the patient and plan prophylaxis before surgery on the predisposed fellow eye.
Delaying definitive vitrectomy in phakic or refractory cases and allowing prolonged corneal-lens touch.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Glaucoma
management: Begin intense cycloplegia with atropine to tighten the zonules and rotate the ciliary body posteriorly, re-establishing forward aqueous flow
Add aqueous suppressants such as topical beta-blockers, alpha-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, with hyperosmotic agents to shrink the vitreous and lower pressure
Avoid miotics such as pilocarpine, which paradoxically worsen the block
Use Nd:YAG laser disruption of the anterior hyaloid and posterior capsule, with argon laser to the ciliary processes, when medical therapy fails
Proceed to pars plana vitrectomy with anterior hyaloid disruption, often combined with irido-zonulo-hyaloidectomy, for refractory cases
Exclude mimics including pupillary block, suprachoroidal haemorrhage and choroidal effusion before treating
Monitor intraocular pressure and anterior chamber depth for recurrence and take preventive precautions in the fellow eye during any future intraocular surgery
